stories.headline: California prosecutors, victim advocates challenge Newsom's mass death sentence commutation
stories.note: Prosecutors and victims' families are pushing back on Newsom's move to spare death row inmates, keeping him on the defensive over crime.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom's blanket commutation of 548 California death sentences to life without parole is drawing fire from prosecutors and crime victims' advocates, who say the move shut grieving families out of the clemency process entirely.

Modoc County District Attorney Nina Salarno, whose own sister was murdered in 1979, met with President Trump in Washington this week alongside other advocates. She argued every case deserved individual review and called the blanket order "offensive to our entire rule of law."

Topo Padilla of Crime Victims United pointed out that California voters have repeatedly kept the death penalty, including a 2016 measure meant to speed up executions. On Nov. 16, roughly 30 county DAs, law enforcement groups, advocates and families asked the California Supreme Court to halt the commutations. Trump, for his part, said he will have the Justice Department seek the death penalty for child murderers and speed up federal executions.
Newsom's office pointed to a release featuring victims and survivors who back his decision, including Rabbi Suzanne Singer, who said she opposes the death penalty and praised the governor.

Why it matters: Newsom is weighing a 2028 run, and this fight puts him on the side of convicted killers against voters, prosecutors and victims' families, a law-and-order contrast Republicans are eager to highlight.

stories.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García lands in Spain, ending deportation battle with Trump administration
stories.note: The illegal immigrant Democrats made a cause célèbre is now out of the country, a win for the Trump administration's deportation push.
body: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran illegal immigrant whose case became a rallying cry for critics of Trump's immigration enforcement, landed in Madrid on Wednesday after agreeing to leave the United States. His lawyers told The New York Times he ultimately plans to go to Mexico.

Sources said a federal judge in Maryland had ordered him to leave by Tuesday; that order remains sealed. DHS stressed he left under a removal order, paid for his own flight, received no self-deportation incentives, and will never be allowed back.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin celebrated the departure, repeating the administration's claims that Ábrego García is a gang member and abuser. Karoline Leavitt said the outcome "vindicated" the administration.

Democrats saw it differently. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who visited him in El Salvador, said he leaves as a free man and that the administration was forced into a deal respecting his due process. His attorney said they expect a future administration to help bring him back to Maryland.

The case dates to March 2025, when he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador's CECOT prison, then returned to face human smuggling charges that a judge later dismissed. The administration has pointed to alleged MS-13 ties and a 2021 protective order filed by his wife.
Why it matters: Democrats spent enormous political capital defending Ábrego García. His exit lets the administration claim a high-profile win in its deportation push.

stories.headline: ICE nabs illegal immigrant days after he claims $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery prize
stories.note: ICE keeps making arrests in deep-blue Massachusetts, underscoring the administration's enforcement focus.
body: Days after posing with an oversized $1 million check from the Massachusetts State Lottery, Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales was arrested by ICE in East Boston following a brief foot chase early Tuesday, according to three ICE sources who spoke to Fox News.

The sources said the Salvadoran national crossed the border illegally near Roma, Texas, in 2013 and had been wanted under a final deportation order since April 2014. Officers' body cameras recorded the arrest.

The lottery awarded him the prize on Nov. 18 for a winning $10 "$2,000,000 50X Cashword" scratch ticket bought at a market in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he was picked up, and posted his photo on Facebook three days later. The lottery says anyone 18 or older can buy a ticket from a licensed retailer.

Why it matters: A man under a deportation order for more than a decade was living openly in deep-blue Massachusetts. The arrest shows ICE following through on old removal orders, even in sanctuary-minded places.

stories.headline: DOJ recovers $8B, charges more than 800 suspects in largest anti-scam surge in history
stories.note: A record anti-scam crackdown gives the Trump DOJ a big law-and-order result to tout.
body: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Tuesday that federal prosecutors have charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses in the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in Justice Department history.

The push follows President Trump's March executive order directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud. Since then, DOJ has brought more than 400 criminal cases in 85 federal districts. "We are dismantling the criminal networks," Blanche said.

FBI Director Kash Patel described Operation Blackout, which he said has seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 devices, shut down 29 overseas scam compounds on four continents and freed more than 2,200 trafficking victims forced to run the schemes.

Targets ranged from inmates running jury-duty extortion scams on contraband phones to cartel-linked timeshare fraud in Mexico. Through Operation Level Up with the Secret Service, Patel said agents stopped nearly $700 million in losses across 11,000 Americans, most of whom didn't know they were being scammed.

Why it matters: With Blanche citing a Gallup finding that 10% of Americans were hit by a scam in 2025, a record crackdown that returns money to victims gives the administration a concrete, nonpartisan-sounding win on protecting families and seniors.

stories.headline: Kamala Harris' former political mentor and boyfriend delivers stinging warning about 2028 comeback
stories.note: Even an old ally is warning Harris against a 2028 comeback, another sign of Democrats' messy bench.
body: Willie Brown, the former San Francisco mayor and California Assembly speaker who helped launch Kamala Harris' career, says he doesn't want her to run for president in 2028.

In an interview with independent journalist Tara Palmeri, Brown said Harris is "not a communicator" and added, "I'm sorry that she even thinks about running for president." He said she has already reached the highest office any woman in America has held.
Brown appointed Harris to two state boards early in her career, helped her first race for San Francisco district attorney, and dated her in 1994 and 1995, something he has openly written about.

Harris' representatives didn't respond to Fox News Digital. She hasn't announced 2028 plans and said earlier this year that she goes "back and forth." Meanwhile, Ro Khanna, Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom are all signaling interest.
Why it matters: When one of Harris' oldest political patrons publicly doubts her, it underscores how unsettled and crowded the Democrats' 2028 field already is.

stories.headline: Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy
stories.note: Biden's weak library fundraising highlights how little enthusiasm remains for his legacy among Democratic donors.
body: Tax filings show Joe Biden's presidential library foundation raised just $1.5 million in 2025, his first year out of office. Barack Obama raised $232.6 million in his first year, so Biden pulled in less than 1% of that.

The Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation still hasn't picked a site and spent about $600,000 more than it raised last year. A library official told CBS News it wasn't actively fundraising in 2025, and a source said it brought in several multimillion-dollar gifts in 2026, including two $5 million donations.

Some Biden allies are reportedly frustrated that Democratic donors haven't stepped up. Supporters point to the end of the COVID pandemic and major legislation as lasting accomplishments, while a January 2025 Gallup poll found 54% of adults expected history to rate him below average or poor.
Heritage Action's Doug Blair called the weak haul "a fitting bookend for a failed presidency." Neither the Biden nor Obama foundations responded to Fox News Digital.
Why it matters: Even Democratic donors seem ready to move on from Biden, a reminder of how badly his single term is regarded.

stories.headline: Marco Rubio's 2028 stock surges among House Republicans as Trump insiders split on Vance
stories.note: The GOP has a deep 2028 bench, with Rubio gaining momentum alongside Vance.
body: After the GOP's 2026 midterm losses, a growing number of House Republicans are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028, Fox News Digital reports.

Rep. Nicole Malliotakis called Rubio "the whole package" and said he could win back Hispanic voters. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, a Freedom Caucus founder, said he's "all in for Marco," and Florida Reps. Carlos Gimenez and Mike Haridopolos said many colleagues have come to them offering support.

Backers pointed to Rubio's recent Athens speech calling for a renewal of Western civilization as a sign of his presidential appeal. Rubio himself has publicly brushed off talk about his political future.

Inside the administration, officials described staff as roughly split 50/50 between Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. Trump said over the weekend that both are "doing fantastically" and very popular.
Why it matters: As Republicans regroup, having two strong, popular contenders gives the party a deep bench heading into 2028.
